abstract: M. Hewitt: Regarding Mr Weaving's reply to Mr G. D. Walker's remarks on transformers with their windings screened by metallized paper, it is my impression that this reply is based on some misconception formed as a result of Mr Walker's wording, from which Mr Weaving apparently inferred that the individual turns had metallized paper applied to them, which is not the case, at any rate as far as multilayer cross-over type coils are concerned. For such coils “the unit” as far as shielding is concerned is a whole layer or even groups of layers and not individual turns.

articleTitle: The transient voltage characteristics of transformer windings
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper sets out to give a practical explanation of the phenomena that occur in transformer windings subjected to surges. The standing wave and travelling wave theories are outlined and experimental voltage distribution curves shown. The effect and desirability of end-turn reinforcement and methods of increasing the surge strength of transformers, with particular reference to shielding, are discussed. Experimental results of the effect of shielding are given. The conclusion advocates that when purchasing transformers the design of the windings should be left to the manufacturer and a guaranteed surge strength specified.

articleTitle: Discussion on a lightning warning device
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I was interested to read this paper in which an account is given of the utilization of the steady and transient currents in an earth-connected aerial to provide an audible warning of the likelihood of nearby or distant lightning discharges. It may be of some interest to draw attention to a device developed in Great Britain during the last war for use in the operation of the balloon barrage which formed an important part of the aerial-defence system of the country. The device was fitted to the flying cables of certain selected balloons at the periphery of most of the balloon barrages, and was meant to provide an audible warning of an approaching thunderstorm to a barrage controller so that orders could be issued for the close-hauling of balloons if circumstances permitted.

abstract: Of all our five senses, the sense of hearing is perhaps the most used and the most abused. Most used because we cannot shut out a sound as we can cut off an unpleasant sight by closing our eyes, and we are compelled to hear even while we sleep. Abused because so much of the sound we hear is excessively loud and unpleasant, and abused because our ears are so tolerant that we can accustom ourselves without great difficulty to an unnecessary background of noise with out apparently being aware of it, or we can listen to speech or music so distorted during its passage to our ears that it bears very little relation to the original speech and music.

articleTitle: Some factors affecting the design of electric lighting installations for building interiors
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The author examines the methods which should be adopted in order to answer the various questions which an engineer should ask himself when designing an electric lighting installation. The paper stresses the importance of careful tusk analysis in the first instance to determine exactly what is the visual problem for which suitable lighting must be provided, and goes on to discuss methods of lighting, factors affecting illumination requirements, the selection of appropriate lighting fittings and lamps, and the calculations necessary to determine their location and wattage. The paper also deals with probable trends in lighting in the post-war period and the light sources and materials for light control that are likely to influence them.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper deals with electric melting furnaces mainly from the view point of the electrical engineer. It describes the seven main types which have become established and standardised. It covers questions which are often raised by electric supply engineers in relation to the kind of load which these furnaces take from the electric mains. Some notes on working conditions have also been included. A special protective system for high frequency furnaces has been described in some detail; also an all-electric regulator for are furnaces with an indication of the historical background in the development of this apparatus. The paper does not dealwith the electrical theory on which the various furnace designs are based, nor with metallurgical matters, refractory linings, thermal efficiencies and such like; these matters have already beenwell covered elsewhere, especially with respect to high frequency (coreless induction) furnaces and arc furnaces.

articleTitle: Lightning investigation on an 88-kV transmission line in Southern Rhodesia
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Lightning investigation with magnetic link equipment was carried out over two seasons on an 84-mile length of transmission line and over 100 records of lightning currents were obtained. Part I of this paper deals with the characteristics of lightning, its frequency in relation to types of geological formation, and its severity. Support was found for the theory that the type of ground exerted influence upon the frequency of lightning and some outstanding electrical properties of soils were measured and have been outlined. Part II discusses the effect of lightning on transmission lines and a method is given for the prediction of the probability of interruption of supply. Measures taken to improve the lightning performance of the line are described together with calculations concerning the extent of the increased protection there by afforded.

articleTitle: Modern developments in high-voltage cable design and practice, with special reference to the impregnated pressure cable
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The steady improvement and technical development of transmission systems including underground cable is a matter of increasing importance. This is well illustrated by the statistics showing the relative development of the generating side and the transmission side of the English electrical system. Since the Central Electricity Board was formed in 1926 there has been in England a national control of the generation and bulk distribution of electricity. During the following 11 years the average consumption of coal was reduced from 3.4 lb to 1.42 lb per unit generated. At the same time, the cost of generation was reduced from 0.93 pence to 0.29 pence per unit. These figures are all taken from the annual report of the Electricity Commissioners. Unfortunately detailed figures are not available later than 1937, but so far as generation is concerned, the improvement is a very remarkable achievement.

articleTitle: Arc-suppression coils and their application on the systems operated by the victoria falls and transvaal power company, limited
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The general problem of neutral earthing on a high-voltage network is briefly considered. The behaviour of a system earthed through an arcsuppression coil is studied for single-phase fault and the effect of coil tuning on the fault suppression efficiency of the coil discussed. Neutral voltages due to capacity unbalances and also the influencing effect of adjacent parallel lines are analyzed. Applications of arc-suppression coils to th 20-, 40- and 88-kV systems of the Victoria Falls and Transvaal Power Co., Ltd., are discussed and difficulties encountered with the application of unit coils to part of an 88-kV transmission network described. Statistics are given of the operating experience with the coils.
